text: The Romans wrote about almost everything. How to build. How to run an army. Even what to eat.
But they never once mentioned these.
Across the old northern provinces of the empire, archaeologists have found about a hundred and thirty of them. Hollow, cast in bronze.
Twelve flat faces, each one a pentagon. A knob on every corner. And a hole in every face.
But the holes are not the same size.
One found in Hertfordshire, England, in twenty eighteen is eighty-two millimetres across. Its holes range from under fourteen millimetres to twenty.

text: The smallest are about four centimetres, the size of a golf ball. The largest, eleven. Nearly a grapefruit.
asr: The smallest are about 4 centimeters, the size of a golf ball. The largest, 11, nearly a grapefruit.

text: And yet, no Roman text describes them. No painting shows one. No carving depicts one.
Historians have thrown every theory at them. Candle holders. Surveying tools. Dice. Even a gadget for knitting gloves.
Every theory has a problem. A measuring tool should be standard, but no two of these are made the same.
The Hunt Museum in Ireland holds another one. Its catalogue says it plainly: there is no mention of them in classical sources, and their purpose remains unclear.

text: And several were found buried in hoards of coins. You don't bury a candle holder with your life savings.

text: Whoever owned these thought they mattered. And then they vanished from history, leaving us nothing but the objects themselves.
